title: The Mystery of Why Some Drugs Vanish - Nautilus
gist: Disappearing polymorphs, in which a more stable crystal form of a drug emerges and makes the original form apparently impossible to produce worldwide, are a recurring manufacturing and legal hazard for pharma. Abbott's ritonavir lost an estimated $250 million when Form II displaced Form I in 1998, and Glaxo litigated Zantac forms. A 2024 paper recreated ritonavir Form I via ball-mill grinding.

themes.theme: Disappearing polymorphs as a manufacturing risk

insights.claim: In drug manufacturing, a different crystal form (polymorph) of a drug frequently appears during crystallization even when a known process is followed exactly.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Polymorph risk is an underappreciated operational hazard for drugmakers that can halt supply.
insights.quote: And yet this exact scenario happens in drug manufacturing with alarming frequency.

insights.claim: A new polymorph can share the same chemical formula but have a slightly different shape that gives it dramatically different properties.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Identical chemistry does not guarantee identical efficacy, affecting bioavailability and product quality.
insights.quote: It may have the same chemical formula, but this new polymorph has a slightly different shape that gives it dramatically different properties.

insights.claim: Once a new polymorph appears, the original form can seem to vanish from every lab, and even bringing old product into a lab that made the new form can convert it.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Contamination can be global and irreversible, so a single event can threaten a product line everywhere.
insights.quote: In some cases, even bringing the old polymorph to a lab that’s made the new polymorph is enough to make that product transform as well.

insights.claim: Abbott Laboratories' HIV/AIDS antiretroviral ritonavir, approved in 1996 and sold as Form I gel capsules, was superseded by a less soluble Form II in 1998 that rendered it ineffective.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Canonical example of polymorph-driven product failure for a major drugmaker.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most famous disappearing polymorph

insights.claim: Abbott had to pull ritonavir from the market until reformulating it as a caplet in 1999, at an estimated cost of $250 million plus tens of thousands of patients going without medication.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Quantifies the financial and reputational downside of polymorph failure: recalls, lost revenue, reformulation.

insights.claim: Disappearing polymorphs create legal headaches, as shown when Glaxo sued a Canadian company seeking to produce off-patent Form I of ranitidine (Zantac).
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Polymorph patents are a tool for brands to extend exclusivity against generics.
insights.locator: Disappearing polymorphs cause plenty of legal

insights.claim: Glaxo, holding patents on both Form I and Form II of ranitidine, argued that any attempt to make Form I would inevitably contain traces of patented Form II, but lost the suit.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Courts have limited how far polymorph patents can block generic entry, relevant to evergreening strategies.
insights.locator: Disappearing polymorphs cause plenty of legal

insights.claim: Researchers in solid-state chemistry attribute vanishing polymorphs to thermodynamics: the first form may be less stable but faster to form, until a more stable form emerges and takes over.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Implies early-to-market drug forms may be metastable, a latent risk to quality and supply.
insights.quote: The first version of a drug might be a less thermodynamically stable version, but one that forms more quickly.
insights.locator: So why do these polymorphs vanish

insights.claim: Crystals grow via nucleation, so if Form I nucleates faster it can predominate until the more stable Form II appears and dominates.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Process control around nucleation is central to robust pharmaceutical manufacturing.
insights.locator: So why do these polymorphs vanish

insights.claim: The most compelling, though speculative, explanation for worldwide disappearance is that tiny seed molecules of the stable form float in the atmosphere, and a single molecule can kickstart crystallization.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: If airborne seeding is real, contamination control and isolated facilities become strategic manufacturing assets.
insights.quote: there are tiny seed molecules of these drugs just floating around in the atmosphere

insights.claim: Anecdotally, researchers transferred from Form II labs to Form I labs seemed to carry the 'curse' of Form II with them, and some Form I drugs transformed just by sharing a lab with Form II.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Personnel and facility cross-contamination is a practical risk vector for manufacturers.

insights.claim: Disappearing polymorphs are a relatively new phenomenon and an active area of research.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Expect ongoing research spend and potential tooling for solid-form screening.

insights.claim: Researchers have sometimes recreated vanished polymorphs in labs protected from atmospheric and accidental contamination.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Contamination-controlled facilities offer a path to recover lost drug forms.

insights.claim: A 2024 paper recreated Form I of ritonavir via ball-mill grinding, suggesting vanished polymorphs may not be lost for good.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Mechanochemical methods could restore lost formulations, reducing the permanence of polymorph risk.
